paper_title: Extreme Compression of Per-Layer Embeddings via Cross-Layer Latent Vector Quantization

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Scaling embedding capacity alongside Transformer computation is an emerging trend in language models. This trend makes high compression rates increasingly useful. Hence, we study extreme compression of Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), which follow this trend and account for 35.2% of the parameters of Gemma 4 E4B. At such rates, conventional quantizers give each token-layer vector its own code of only a few bytes. We instead develop OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes), which stores one quantized code tuple per token and decodes it at every layer with a layer-specific affine decoder. Codes and decoders are fitted to the PLE output path rather than to the stored vectors. At about $100\times$ PLE compression of bfloat16 (BF16) E4B, OPTIC retains an aggregate 97.8% of the uncompressed model's performance across seven benchmarks, whereas product quantization, the strongest of six conventional baselines, retains 66.3%. At $594\times$ and $1,002\times$ PLE compression of BF16 E4B, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. On the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about $100\times$ PLE compression. During inference at about $100\times$ PLE compression, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory than with uncompressed PLE at the same key-value cache size, while running at most 0.40% slower.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Embedding capacity is emerging as distinct scaling dimension in recent language-model development. Over-Tokenized Transformers (Huang et al., 2025) and SCONE (Yu et al., 2026) scale multi-gram or contextual n-gram representations; DeepSeeks Engram uses hash-addressed n-gram lookup memory (Cheng et al., 2026); and Qwen3.8Flash-Next supplements 125B-parameter lan- *Corresponding author. 1Code: https://github.com/VILA-Lab/optic 1 guage model with 51B parameters of n-gram embeddings (Qiu et al., 2026). Gemma 4 follows this broader direction with Per-Layer Embeddings (PLE), first introduced in Gemma 3n (Gemma Team, 2025), which provide every vocabulary item with learned vector at each decoder layer (Team et al., 2026). We study Gemma 4 E2B and E4B for their strong performance and potential for practical deployment (Team et al., 2026). PLE accounts for 45.8% and 35.2% of the two checkpoints, respectively, making it substantial target for storage reduction as models expand their embedding capacity. An ordinary input embedding maps token to one vector at the models input. PLE provides separate vector at each decoder layer: E4B stores 11 million tokenlayer vectors of width 256, and near 100 compression leaves about five bytes for each. Conventional quantizers spend these bytes on separate code for every vector. OPTIC (Output-Path-fitted, Token-shared Indexed Codes) builds on two observations. First, PLE stores one vector for every pair of token and layer, so compact representation can share storage along either index. OPTIC shares along both. All tokens of layer use one layer-specific affine decoder, whose storage does not grow with the vocabulary size. All layers of token use one code tuple, so tokens bytes form one larger code instead of many small per-layer codes, and the layer decoders preserve the differences between layers. Second, the model uses PLE vectors through gate and an output projection. The fitting objective should therefore account for reconstruction error after the gate and output projection, rather than only in the stored coordinates. OPTIC fits its codes and decoders to minimize error at the projection output. We report performance retention across seven benchmarks relative to the same checkpoint with uncompressed PLE. At about 100 PLE compression, OPTIC retains 97.8% on BF16 E4B, whereas the strongest of six conventional baselines retains 66.3%. With OPTICs fitting recipe and nearly equal storage, independent latent codes for each tokenlayer vector retain 79.3% (Section 5.2). At 594 and 1, 002 PLE compression, where about one byte or less remains for each vector, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1%. In addition, on the official E4B release with 4-bit linear weights and 16-bit activations (W4A16), OPTIC retains 96.9% at about 100 PLE compression, compared with 82.8% for the strongest conventional baseline. On the smaller E2B, OPTIC retains 89.1% on BF16 and 91.5% on the official W4A16 release. model compressed with OPTIC also supports inference directly from the compact codes. On an RTX 4090 with fixed keyvalue cache size, compact PLE lowers the GPU memory of BF16 E4B serving by 29.7% and adds at most 0.40% wall time (Section 6).

sections.title: 2.5 Additional Compact Representations
sections.content: Output-path-weighted PCA-PQ stores one code tuple per tokenlayer row. It scales each row with diagonal output-path weights and then applies PCA and product quantization (PQ). Appendix gives its derivation and fitting procedure, and Appendix A.3 gives its complete storage cost. The frequency-tiered variant of OPTIC gives more code groups to frequent tokens. Every token stores M0 base groups, and the Nfreq most frequent non-special tokens in fixed fitting stream store M1 M0 additional groups. Other tokens use learned shared codeword in each additional group, so every vocabulary item keeps an explicit code. The variant also stores INT8 decoder weights and keeps special-token rows exactly in bfloat16. Appendix A.3 gives its complete storage cost.

sections.title: 3.1 Baselines
sections.content: We evaluate six baselines adapted to the PLE setting: flattened row-wise product quantization 4 (PQ) (Jegou et al., 2010), greedy residual vector quantization (RVQ) (Chen et al., 2010), parametric optimized product quantization (OPQ-P) (Ge et al., 2013), Additive Quantization (AQ) (Babenko and Lempitsky, 2014), the AQLM Euclidean beam encoder (Egiazarian et al., 2024), and post-hoc INT8 randomized low-rank singular value decomposition (SVD) (Halko et al., 2011). Our methods are output-path-weighted PCA-PQ and OPTIC. Each baseline is applied to the PLE tensor under matched resident-byte accounting, and Appendix A.2 gives its representation and fitting rule.

Because the natural text covers only part of the vocabulary, we add one synthetic record for every token in the vocabulary. Repeated special-token records give the fitting procedure additional coverage of tokens used to control generation. Natural records use gates collected from the frozen model, whereas synthetic records use all-ones gates with the same frozen projections. The frequency-tiered variant uses token counts from fitting stream that combines these text sources with text generated by the uncompressed checkpoint. Output-path-weighted PCA-PQ uses the WikiText-2 training split (Merity et al., 2016) for its fitting statistics. Calibration data exclude evaluation examples.

sections.title: 3.3 Evaluation Protocol
sections.content: The seven tasks cover reasoning with PIQA (Bisk et al., 2020), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), GPQA Diamond (Rein et al., 2023) and AIME 2026 (Dekoninck et al., 2026); world knowledge with MMLU-Redux (Hendrycks et al., 2020; Gema et al., 2025); instruction following with IFBench (Pyatkin et al., 2026); and vision with InfographicVQA (Mathew et al., 2022). For each model size and weight format, all methods use the same backbone weights, prompts, generation settings and scorers. The main comparisons use fitting seed 0, and every fit is evaluated after its last scheduled update. Appendix B.2 gives sample counts and evaluation seeds.

sections.title: 4.1 Compression and Quality
sections.content: Table 1 compares methods near 100 PLE compression. OPTIC gives the highest E4B retention: 97.8% on BF16 and 96.9% on W4A16. These E4B results lead the strongest baseline by 31.5 and 14.0 percentage points, respectively. The frequencytiered variant of OPTIC gives the highest E2B retention: 90.0% on BF16 and 93.0% on W4A16. The per-task scores show where the E4B gains arise. On BF16 E4B, OPTIC preserves GSM8K accuracy at 92.8%, compared with 92.9% for uncompressed PLE and 73.5% for PQ. Its IFBench score is 41.7%, compared with 44.0% for uncompressed PLE and 16.0% for PQ. InfographicVQA follows the same pattern: 67.5% for OPTIC, 69.7% for uncompressed PLE and 38.4% for PQ. PIQA changes little for either compressed method. The aggregate advantage includes gains in mathematical reasoning, instruction following and visual question answering. Appendix reports every task score. Table 2 gives 95% paired-bootstrap intervals. The E4B BF16 interval is 95.599.0% for OPTIC and 60.670.5% for PQ. The corresponding W4A16 intervals are 93.997.8% and 76.887.1% for OPTIC and the AQLM Euclidean beam encoder. The intervals remain separated in both E2B settings as well. sections.title: 4.2 Compression Range
sections.content: Figure 2 compares OPTIC with PQ, OPQ-P and output-path-weighted PCA-PQ across five nominal tiers on BF16 E4B. OPTIC has compression ratios of 594 and 1002 at the nominal 500 and 1000 tiers. At these ratios, it retains 90.5% and 84.1% on BF16 E4B and 87.7% and 81.8% on W4A16 E4B  (Table 16)  . Output-path-weighted PCA-PQ is an outputaware row-wise method. It retains 93.3% near 100 on BF16 E4B, 25.1% near 500 and zero near 1000, while OPTIC remains above 84%. The advantage of OPTIC over this row-wise method therefore grows as fewer bytes are available to represent each PLE vector.

sections.title: 5.1 PLE Structure
sections.content: We examine the importance and dimensional structure of token-specific variation in PLE, using the original BF16 E4B table with equal weighting over vocabulary items (Appendix E.3). Each vector etℓ splits into its layers vocabulary mean and centered remainder. The means account for 8.1% of the tables squared Frobenius norm. Replacing every vector with its layer mean lowers GSM8K from 92.9% to 43.5% and GPQA Diamond from 56.9% to 23.0%; AIME 2026 falls to zero, making seventask retention zero. Layer means alone therefore do not preserve model performance. We next examine whether the remaining variation is concentrated in low-dimensional subspace. Besides the stored coordinates, we use the outputpath metric Gℓ (Equation 6) to account for the gate and projection before normalization. In stored coordinates, capturing 90% of layers token-specific variation requires 212227 of 256 principal directions. Under the output-path metric, it requires 1205 directions (median 158), indicating substantial differences across layers (Figure 3).

sections.title: 7 Related Work
sections.content: Embedding compression. Multi-codebook representations have been used to compress word embeddings for NLP. Shu and Nakayama (2018) learn compositional discrete codes and codebooks for an embedding matrix. Our setting has an additional layer axis: the same vocabulary item has different embedding at each layer. We exploit this correspondence by decoding one token representation into multiple layer-specific rows. CARVQ combines grouped residual codes with nonlinear corrective adaptor for ordinary token embeddings (Gou et al., 2025); our representation instead shares tokens latent codes across layers. Vector quantization and low-rank representations. Product quantization divides vector into subspaces and quantizes each subspace (Jegou et al., 2010); optimized product quantization learns transformation before quantization (Ge et al., 2013). Residual and additive quantizers represent vectors through sums of codewords (Chen et al., 2010; Babenko and Lempitsky, 2014). Low-rank factorization instead stores continuous coordinates and shared basis; randomized SVD offers practical fitting procedure (Halko et al., 2011). OPTIC combines shared latent representation with discrete token codes and layer-specific affine decoders. This shares the code storage across layers while keeping separate reconstruction map for each layer. Output-aware model compression. Weight reconstruction can account for models inputs and activations. GPTQ uses approximate secondorder information for post-training weight quantization (Frantar et al., 2022), while AWQ uses activation statistics to choose channel scales that protect salient weights (Lin et al., 2024). AQLM combines input-adaptive additive quantization with joint block optimization (Egiazarian et al., 2024). Our loss follows the gated PLE output path instead of linear weight matrix. Compressing this separate embedding table complements backbone weight quantization, as our BF16 and W4A16 experiments demonstrate. Our comparisons include the AQLM Euclidean beam encoder and output-path-fitted additive codes; Appendices and give their PLE adaptations and storage budgets.

sections.title: 8 Conclusion
sections.content: OPTIC stores one code tuple per token, which every layer decodes through its own affine decoder, and fits codes and decoders at the PLE projection output, before normalization. Near 100 PLE compression, it achieves seven-task retention of 97.8% on BF16 E4B and 96.9% on W4A16 E4B. Independent latent codes for each vector retain 79.3% on BF16 E4B with nearly equal storage. At 594 and 1002 PLE compression, OPTIC retains 90.5% and 84.1% of BF16 E4B performance, respectively. Served directly from OPTIC codes with fixed keyvalue cache size, BF16 E4B uses 29.7% less GPU memory with at most 0.40% added wall time. These results show substantial compression potential in Gemma 4s expanded embedding tables. They motivate designing embedding capacity and compressed representations together, with deployment memory as constraint. Our BF16 and W4A16 results show that PLE compression complements backbone quantization; extending this combination to other embedding structures is promising direction.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: The study evaluates PLE in Gemma 4 E2B and E4B. The main comparisons and Table 3 use one fixed fitting seed, so the paired-bootstrap intervals describe benchmark sampling uncertainty. The three-fit comparisons and controls describe fitting variation under the common Euclidean initialization. At matched byte budget, removing code sharing also changes how bytes are divided between codes and decoders, so the code-sharing ablation measures this combined effect with the fitting recipe held fixed. The fixed-code objective ablation applies to continuous fitting, and the output-path loss holds the gates fixed and measures error only at each layers projection output. The baselines, including the AQLM Euclidean beam encoder, are adaptations of their original methods to PLE. single low-count task can strongly affect retention.

sections.title: Ethical Considerations
sections.content: Compression reduces the resources needed to study and deploy existing models. It can broaden access to model research, although the same resource savings can also lower the cost of harmful applications. AI assistants were used for language polishing and code assistance. The authors remain responsible for the results, references, implementation and writing.

B.1 Fitting Procedure OPTIC and its frequency-tiered variant use seed 0, PCA initialization weighted by the output-path objective, 25 iterations of K-means codebook initialization, and fixed 5,000-step AdamW schedule. The BF16 E4B nominal-100 configuration has latent width 644, 161 groups, 256 codewords per group and codeword width four. Continuous updates use learning rate 3 104, zero weight decay, batches of 8,192 positions and gradient clipping at norm one. We set λ in Equation 7 to 108 times the mean diagonal entry of (cid:80) ℓ GℓAℓ. Two reassignment sweeps follow updates 500, 1000, . . . , 4500. After reassignment, unused codewords are initialized from tokens with large quantization errors, and their optimizer moments are reset. Each fit runs all 5,000 updates, and the state after the last update is the reported artifact. ℓ AT B.2 Models and Evaluation The experiment crosses two Gemma 4 scales (Team et al., 2026) with the original BF16 releases (Google DeepMind, 2026a,d) and official W4A16 releases (Google DeepMind, 2026c,f).
